Where it began

Gudakesh Motie was born in Georgetown on 29 March 1995 and has played his domestic cricket for Guyana. He bowls left-arm orthodox spin and bats in the lower order. In 2014 he went to the Under-19 World Cup, held in the United Arab Emirates, with the West Indies side.

His first-class debut came for Guyana in November 2015, against the Windward Islands. It took him just one match to find his feet, and then the wickets came in a flood. In his second, against the Leeward Islands, he took 6 for 20 and 5 for 85, eleven wickets in the match, and was named man of the match. Two more six-wicket hauls followed that season, against Barbados and Jamaica.

The player

White-ball cricket came next. In the 2021 Super50 nobody took more wickets than his 16. He played for the Guyana Amazon Warriors in the Caribbean Premier League, and made his Twenty20 international debut against Pakistan on 16 December 2021.

In May 2022 he hit 110 against Barbados, his first first-class hundred, and the following month he was a Test cricketer, making his debut against Bangladesh on 16 June 2022. His one-day international debut followed against the same opponents in July, and in 2024 West Indies picked him for their T20 World Cup squad.

Between 2022 and 2025 he played 11 Tests and took 35 wickets at 27.03, with a best of 7 for 37. Twice he took five wickets in an innings, and once ten in a match.

What made him special

Motie's Test record is that of a bowler who could take a game by the collar: 35 wickets in 11 matches is more than three a Test. On his day he could run through a batting side, as his early haul for Guyana showed, and he did it again on the biggest stage when he took ten in a Test.

He was useful with the bat, too. He made 265 Test runs at 22.08 with a top score of 55, and he was not out five times in 17 innings, which tells you he was not easy to shift. A Test hundred never quite came his way, though his hundred against Barbados shows it was not for want of trying. Catches were rarer, five in 11 Tests, as if the ball had somewhere else it would rather be.

And finally

His maiden first-class hundred came only a month before his first Test call. Selectors had plenty of reasons to pick a left-arm spinner who took wickets in heaps. Even so, a hundred against Barbados, just as the Test team was being chosen, cannot have hurt his chances. It is a neat way to remind everyone that a spinner can bat.
